### EDA

#### Exploratory

Your task is to understand the basic structure of a new data set from 2020 related to tuition costs at colleges and universities across the country. It is stored as a csv on github that can be read into your R session (or a Quarto document) using:

```{r}
#| message: false
tuition_cost <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-03-10/tuition_cost.csv')
```

For each of the following, please answer the question in full sentences, provide the code that you used, along with the plot (or a sketch of it).

@. What are the dimensions of the data set? What is the unit of observation? What is the nature of the variables (what they are, their units or levels, and their type)?

@. Is there any missing data? If so, where?

@. What is the distribution of the cost of in-state tuition? Answer with summary statistics, a plot, and a written description of its shape.

@. The `type` variable is intended to sort institutions into three types: public, private, and for-profit. Evaluate whether that is true of this data set and let it inform your answer to the next question.

@. How does the distribution of in-state tuition differ between the types of institutions? Answer with a plot and a written description of how the distributions compare.

@. Which are the three most expensive institutions? The three least expensive institutions?

@. Create one more visualization of at least two variables that you're curious about. Describe the structure that you see with a written description. Then write down one new question that your plot raises, one that you would need more digging (or more data) to answer.

#### Explanatory

Each of the plots below is meant to tell a particular story to a particular audience. As you craft them, think carefully about the labels, themes, aesthetic settings, and the manner in which they facilitate comparisons.

@. Return to the tuition data and make two explanatory plots from it, each telling a different story. For each plot, before you write any code, write down a plan like the ones we made for the EV data in class:

    - **Audience:** who is this plot for?
    - **Story:** what is the one thing you want them to take away?
    - **Strategy:** what will you do to the plot to make that story easy to see?

    Then provide the code alongside the plot (or a sketch of it). The two plots should make different comparisons easy, so draw on the tools from class: labels, limits and baselines, non-linear scales, reordering categories with `fct_reorder()` or `fct_infreq()`, themes, and setting aesthetics.

@. Provide the code that will create this plot from the `storms` data set inside the `dplyr` package. A few notes:
    - Each dot is a single *observation* of a storm, not a whole storm: storms are measured every six hours over their lifetimes.
    - You will need to create a new column indicating storm type based on wind speed. For that you'll need to learn how that determination is made and then add it to the data frame. The `case_when()` function is a helpful shortcut similar to `ifelse()`.
    - The color palette belongs to a set of palettes called ColorBrewer. You can read more about them here: <https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/scale_brewer.html>.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-align: center
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

storms2 <- storms |>
  mutate(class = case_when(wind < 34 ~ "Tropical Depression",
                           wind < 64 ~ "Tropical Storm",
                           TRUE ~ "Hurricane")) |>
  mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("Tropical Depression", "Tropical Storm", "Hurricane")))

ggplot(storms2, aes(x = pressure,
                    y = wind,
                    color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "RdPu") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  labs(title = "Wind Speed and Pressure in Storms (1975-2024)",
       x = "Air pressure (mb)",
       y = "Maximum wind speed (knots)",
       color = "Storm type")
```

@. Name at least two changes you'd make to the storms plot to make it easier to read. For each, say which comparison it would make easier to see.

@. Remake your storms plot using a very specific visual theme: the botanical paintings of the US Department of Agriculture. They have been wrapped up into a ggplot2 theme inside the `ggpomological` package: <https://github.com/gadenbuie/ggpomological>. Read about how to use the package and write below the additional layers that you added to your plot above (for a challenge, see if you can get the handwriting font to show up). If you also wanted to tweak your plot with `theme()`, where in your code would that layer need to go, and why?

@. The `present` data frame stores data from the US Census about the number of boys and girls born each year between 1940 and 2013. It is stored in the `stat20data` package, which can be installed from GitHub using the `devtools` package.

    ```{r}
    #| eval: false
    # install.packages("devtools")
    # devtools::install_github("https://github.com/stat20/stat20data")
    library(stat20data)
    slice(present, 1:5)
    ```

    Make two plots of the trend over time in the proportion of births that are girls, each with a horizontal line at a baseline of .5 (see `geom_hline()`).

    - **Plot A:** put the annual variability into context by ensuring the viewer can see the full range of possible values that the proportion could take.
    - **Plot B:** let the y-axis zoom in on the range of the data.

    For each plot, write one sentence giving the story it tells and an audience it would suit.

@. (Challenge) Some of the most effective plots on the web don't come from R or Python, but from dedicated visualization libraries written in JavaScript. That is the case for the EV registration plot made by the Department of Energy (<https://afdc.energy.gov/data/10962>), which uses a library called [Highcharts](https://www.highcharts.com/).

    While you could craft the plot directly using JavaScript, a member of the R community has written a package that allows you to make them directly from R: you write R code, which the package turns into JavaScript, which Highcharts then renders as a plot. Read how to use the package on its documentation site: <https://github.com/jbkunst/highcharter/>.

    Your task is to recreate the EV Highcharts plot exactly using the data found in an excel spreadsheet on the DoE website. You can export the excel spreadsheet as a csv file, as we did in class, or you can experiment with the `readxl` package to read it into R directly.

### Joins

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
roster <- tibble(student_id = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
                 name = c("Ada", "Bruno", "Chandra", "Diego"),
                 major = c("Stat", "DS", "Stat", "Econ"))

grades <- tibble(student_id = c(2, 3, 4, 5),
                 quiz_score = c(88, 94, 77, 91))

roster
grades
```

These data sets illustrate a roster of students registered for a particular lab section (`roster`) and the record of grades on a quiz (`grades`). For each of the following, write appropriate the `dplyr` join command and sketch the resulting data frame that contains those records.

@. All registered students who took the quiz.

@. The quiz scores for all registered students.

@. The names and majors or all students who took the quiz.

@. All records for students either registered for the section or who took the quiz or both.

@. The name and major of the registered students who didn't take the quiz.

The following questions return to the `storms` data found in the `dplyr` package.

@. Calculate the maximum wind speed of each storm, then attach that column of data to the original `storms` data frame.

@. Create a small data frame that you can then use to filter the `storms` data so that it only retains records of storms that are "Hurricanes", "Tropical Storms", and "Tropical Depressions". (note: don't use `filter`!)

@. Create a small data frame that you can use to add on a new column to `storms` called `type` that has levels of "Hurricanes", "Tropical Storms", and "Tropical Depressions" for storms with that `status` and "Other" for all other storms. (note: don't use `mutate()`!)

@. Remake the state-by-state EV registration chart but instead of plotting the distribution of registrations, display, for every state, either: a) the proportion of vehicle registrations that are EV b) the ratio of EV registrations to residents. To do this you will need to track down additional data online and join it with the EV data registration data.

### ...and Pivots

The `tidyr` package contains the following data set called `fish_encounters` collected by aquatic scientist (and Cal grad!) Myfanwy Johnson.

```{r}
library(tidyr)
fish_encounters
```

@. What is the unit of observation? What values are found in the `seen` column? What do they indicate? What values are missing? (see `?fish_encounters`)

@. Some forms of analysis require a format where every row is a unique fish and every column is a monitoring station. Write the code to perform this transformation and sketch the resulting data frame, illustrating the column names, the number of rows, and a sample of the values that are seen.

@. R uses `NA` to indicate a measurement that was intended to be taken but that is missing for whatever reason. In this case, that absence means that in fact the fish was not detected, so the value should really be a `0`. Revisit your `pivot_()` command and add an additional argument to fill those values with `0` instead of `NA` (see the help file for pivot).

@. Reshape your new data frame back to the shape of the original `fish_encounters`. What are the dimensions and how does it compare to the original data frame?

The package also contains a data frame called `billboard`, which records the billboard rankings of different songs in 2000.

```{r}
library(tidyr)
billboard
```

@. What are the dimensions of the data frame? What are the values stored in the `wk` columns? Why does it have `wk76` column? Weren't there only 52 weeks in 2000? (see `?billboard`)

@. This data frame possess a strange quality: the week data is stored across column names instead of in the values of a column called `week`. Pivot `billboard` to create this alternative (more useful) representation^[Hint: there is a handy shortcut that saves you from typing all of the column names: `starts_with()` inside the `tidyselect` package]. Make a sketch of the data frame, indicate its dimensions and the columns that it contains.

@. Remove all rows from the new data frame that are unranked in a given week. This can either be done using `drop_na()` or more elegantly back in your `pivot_()` function by adding another argument that takes care of it (see the help file for ideas). Provide the code that you used here.

@. Using this reshaped data frame, make a line plot^[Note that `geom_line()` permits the use of a `group` aesthetic mapping to make one line for each group.] that shows how each track moves through ranks from one week to the next. Provide the code used to construct your plot as well as a sketch of the result.

To really polish your graphic:

   - Add transparency to the lines to prevent overplotting
   - Add useful labels
   - Modify the theme if you wish
   - *Challenge*: Invert the y-axis so that the top ranks (lowest numbers) are at the top of the y-axis.
   - *Challenge*: Similar to the COVID plot seen in lecture, pick one line to highlight in a bright color and color the rest of the lines a more subtle color. This could be your favorite track, an example of a "slow burn" track that took a long time to reach the top, a "flash in the pan" track that gained fast and faded fast, or the track that stayed at number 1 for the longest.

### Strings I

The following questions concern the R object called `fruit` that is stored in the `stringr` package.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(stringr)
head(fruit)
```

@. What data structure is `fruit` and what is its length?

@. Which fruits have the longest and shortest names?

@. Replace the entry `"currant"` with `"red currant"`.

@. Form a single string that starts with `"My favorite fruits are"` and then lists all of the fruits, separated by a comma and a space. The end of the list should have `"and"` before the last fruit and end with a period.

@. Form a string like the following but with another fruit and emoji^[Each emoji is defined by an 8 digit code called Unicode. See <https://r4ds.hadley.nz/strings.html#other-special-characters>.] of your choice. Note the fruit name should come directly from `fruit`.

```{r}
#| echo: false

paste("\U0001f34b", fruit[44], "\U0001f34b")
```

@. Print all of the fruit names containing `"berry"`.

@. How many fruit names contain the letter `"o"`?

@. Which fruit names contain the most `"o"`s?^[Write a pattern that matches only names with at least two `"o"`s, using the wildcard and a quantifier. Then extend it to three, four, and so on until nothing matches.]

@. How many fruits feature two `"a"`s separated by one other character?

@. Create the string below and print it with `str_view()`. Then print it again in all capital letters.

```{r}
#| echo: false
str_view("The sign said \"Fresh fruit!\"\nand we believed it.")
```

@. Abbreviate each fruit name to its first three letters. Which fruits have an abbreviation with two vowels in a row? Use a character class and a quantifier in your pattern.

### Dates and Times I

The next few questions reference the moment that the ball fully dropped in Times Square in New York City at the first moment of the new year in 2000. The corresponding UNIX time was 946684800. Please form a vector to captures this point in time in several different ways. Remember you may need to look at function help files to learn more about how the functions taught in class work.

@. Using baseR and the Unix epoch.

@. Using baseR and a string that expresses the timepoint in a format similar to `"2026-10-14 13:00:00"`.

@. Using baseR and a string that expresses the timepoint in a format similar to `"Oct 14, 2026 1:00 pm"`.

@. Using lubridate and a string that expresses the timepoint in a format similar to `"2026-10-14 13:00:00"`.

@. Using lubridate and a string that expresses the timepoint in a format similar to `"Oct 14, 2026 1:00 pm"`.

@. What is the type of the objects created by the different commands used above?

### Dates and Times II

Using the notions of durations, periods, and timezones from `lubridate`, provide the code and output to answer the following questions.

@. How old are you? Answer as a duration.

@. How old will you be in one month? Answer both using durations and periods.

@. What time is it now? Answer using the `now()` function in lubridate and answer in HH:MM:SS and provide the timezone.

@. What is the current time in UTC (the time in London during winter)?

@. Now imagine you call your friend right now in Delhi, India and ask them to do the same on their phone. What will they say? (in HH:MM:SS with timezone).

* * *

These exercises will be easiest done iteratively in R. You can copy your answers back here or produce your problem set document using Quarto directly. The data set at hand is called `flights` inside the `nycflights` package.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)    # this is also in library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13) # install this if you don't have it
flights               # take a glimpse at the data frame
```

@. Start by reading the documention for the data frame. What is the unit of observation? What time span and geography is covered by this data? Which time zones are any time columns recorded in?

@. Using `year`, `month`, `day`, and the integer clock times `sched_dep_time` and `dep_time` (HHMM)^[You can parse these clock times using what you know about string manipulation or by using handy math operators `%/%` and `%%`. Another hint: see the Circular Data example from the slides.], add two more variables to your data frame:

    i. `sched_dep_ts`: the scheduled departure timestamp.
    ii. `dep_ts`: the actual wheels-off timestamp.

Both must be POSIXct in the "America/New_York" time zone.

@. Calculate the actual wheels-off timestamp in two additional ways and store them as additional variables in your data frame:
  i. `dep_ts_dur`: add to `sched_dep_ts` the recorded time span of the departure delay as a *duration*.
  ii. `dep_ts_per`: add to `sched_dep_ts` the recorded time span of the departure delay as a *period*.

In general do the different approaches align? How about if you look at the precise edge of a switch to/from Daylight Savings Time?

@. *Challenge*: Construct scheduled and realized arrival timestamps using only columns in flights. Build `sched_arr_ts` from `year`, `month`, `day`, and `sched_arr_time` (HHMM) in "America/New_York".

For red-eyes that arrive after midnight local time, `sched_arr_time` may be smaller than `sched_dep_time`. Correct the date by adding a day to `sched_arr_ts` when needed.

Do the analogous construction for actual `arr_ts` from `arr_time`.

Then compute:

- `sched_block <- as.duration(sched_arr_ts - sched_dep_ts)`
- `actual_block <- as.duration(arr_ts - dep_ts)`

Report the median difference `actual_block` - `sched_block` in minutes.
